rewrites.summary:
American Samoa decriminalised same-sex conduct in its 1979 criminal-code revision, effective 1980, age of consent equal at 16. No local non-discrimination protections exist; birth-record gender markers change only with medical documentation.

Marriage law is a distinctive limbo. The Fono Senate declined to outlaw same-sex marriage in 2003; after the 2015 US Supreme Court ruling the attorney general said applicability was 'still being reviewed' while every other territory adopted it, and a judge confirmed in 2016 said his court 'doesn't deal with this ruling' and refused to perform same-sex weddings. None are performed today; the 2022 federal Respect for Marriage Act forces recognition of unions performed elsewhere, and a 2026 practitioner law review argues the ruling binds ASM — yet no couple has applied for a licence and the litigation route (territorial High Court, then the Interior Department) is untested; a 2024 survey still treats the ban as operative.

Gender diversity has deep roots: fa'afafine, assigned male at birth and embodying both genders, are integral to traditional Samoan culture; their representative society formed in 2010 as cultural reclamation. Travel writing contrasts widely accepted homosexuality in Samoan culture with neighbouring Fiji's hostility; the church-centred society expects reserve. For an outed trans visitor: no criminal law, long social visibility, thin institutional protection, unsettled federal guarantees.
rewrites.blindSummary:
A South Pacific island territory of a large federal republic, partly governed through chiefly custom. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised by a 1979 code revision effective 1980, age of consent equal at 16; there are no local discrimination protections, and birth-record gender markers change only with medical documentation.

Marriage law is an unresolved limbo. The upper legislative chamber declined to outlaw same-sex marriage in 2003; after the republic's 2015 high-court ruling, officials left its applicability 'under review' while every peer territory adopted it, and a judge confirmed in 2016 said the local court 'doesn't deal with this ruling' and refused such weddings. None are performed today; a 2022 federal statute forces recognition of unions performed elsewhere, and a 2026 practitioner law article argues the ruling binds the territory — yet no couple has applied, and a defined litigation path (territorial high court, then the federal territory ministry) is untested; a 2024 survey still treats the local ban as operative.

Gender diversity is long-established: a recognised third-gender presence is integral to traditional culture, formally organised in 2010 as cultural reclamation; travel writing reports widely accepted homosexuality in the local culture, though a reserved, church-centred society expects conformity. For an outed trans visitor: no criminal law, deep social visibility, thin institutional protection, unsettled federal guarantees.
blindSourceSummaries: University research guide (updated 2026) with substantive territory content: the indigenous third-gender community formally organised in 2010 as cultural reclamation; colonial suppression followed by reclaiming of local gender identities.

Travel column (2009): a traditional, reserved society where homosexuality is described as widely accepted in local culture, unlike a neighbouring island nation known for hostility; hotels skew toward business travel.

News report (2015): the federal marriage-equality ruling's applicability to this unincorporated territory was left 'under review' while all peer territories moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made; experts warned the review had a chilling effect.

2003 report: the territory's upper legislative chamber voted down a bill outlawing same-sex marriages before any US state ruling forced the question; gender-variant residents testified they sought no such marriages.

2016 report: a unanimously confirmed former territory attorney general, seated as a district judge, said he had not read the US marriage-equality ruling, that his court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and he would not perform same-sex weddings unless laws changed.

2026 law-review article by two attorneys practising in the territory: the federal ruling does bind the territory and marriage certificates must be issued to any same-sex couple applying; to date none has applied; litigation route (territorial high court, then the federal department for territories) set out but untested.

2024 on-island survey of a constitutional-law question: nine years after the federal ruling and after a 2022 federal recognition mandate, the local ban is treated as operative on-island and its constitutional durability as an open question.
rewrites.notes: Decriminalisation corrected to 1979/80; 'upheld-ruling' flag recast as operational blockage; ranking language removed.
